337.title: Bo: a sign upon your hand (Exodus 13:9, 16)
337.hook: the Exodus is remembered on the hand and between the eyes, a root of tefillin
337.howItsDone: Jews who keep the practice, traditionally men and in some communities women too, put on tefillin for weekday morning prayer, binding one box on the arm and one on the head; tefillin are not worn on Shabbat or festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, haggadah, the telling, each generation's own story. Your line was tell your child. Today, the last day of Bo, and a memory you wear instead of tell.

A wedding ring. A string on a wrist from a grandmother. A watch that belonged to someone who's gone. A medical bracelet. Some things people remember in their heads, and some on their skin, where their hands brush them again and again without trying. Bo is ending. The plagues are over, the night of the Exodus has come and gone, and the people are finally out. And the portion's last word on the matter isn't a story or a song. It's a sign, worn on the body.
screen: `A RING. A STRING. A WATCH.` → `MEMORY ON THE SKIN.` → `BO ENDS WITH A SIGN.`

segments.voice: Twice, near the end of Bo, the Torah says the Exodus should be remembered on the body. The first time: "And it shall be for a sign unto thee upon thy hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes." A few verses later, it's for a sign upon thy hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes. Jewish tradition reads these verses, and two more in Deuteronomy, as the command of tefillin: two small black leather boxes, one bound on the arm, by tradition facing the heart, one on the head above the forehead, worn in weekday morning prayer. Inside the boxes are four handwritten passages from the Torah. Two are from this very portion, the two you just heard. The other two are from Deuteronomy, the Shema and the paragraph after it. So on weekday mornings the Exodus is literally bound on the arm. The word for frontlets, totafot, is a puzzle; nobody is certain where it comes from. The Talmud plays with it as two foreign words that each mean two, which add up to the four compartments of the head box. Whatever its origin, the idea is plain: memory that lives only in your head fades. Memory bound to your hand and your eyes stays where you'll keep bumping into it. And with that, Bo is done: come, not go; the darkness; the new moon; the telling; and the sign on the hand.

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your other forearm and feel the weight of it. Is there anything you wear that carries a memory, a ring, a bracelet, a scar you've made peace with, a shirt someone gave you? If there is, touch it and let the memory come; if not, choose something now, a hair tie, a watch on the other wrist, and give it a job: to remind you of one thing you've been freed from.
Bo. Come. The portion we finish today, which ends by binding the Exodus to the hand and between the eyes.
Your line: remember with your body. Some memories are worn, not only told. Day three hundred thirty-seven, in the books.

338.title: Beshalach: the long way round (Exodus 13:17)
338.hook: God leads them away from the short road lest they see war and turn back
338.carry: the long way can be kinder
338.howItsDone: Beshalach is read in synagogue in winter, on the Shabbat called Shabbat Shirah, the Sabbath of song, because it contains the Song at the Sea, which the congregation often stands for.

segments.voice: Yesterday Bo ended with a sign upon the hand. Your line was remember with your body. Today, a new portion, and the people's first steps out.

Open a map app and it hands you the fastest route, down to the minute. It doesn't know you hate that interchange. It doesn't know you've only just learned to drive, or that the quick road runs past the house of someone you can't face yet. Sometimes the shortest road is the one most likely to make you turn around. The Israelites are free. They're standing at the edge of Egypt, and the quickest road to the promised land runs straight along the coast. A new portion begins here, and the very first thing it says is that God doesn't take it.
screen: `THE FASTEST ROUTE.` → `THE ROAD THAT MAKES YOU TURN BACK.` → `GOD DOESN'T TAKE IT.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Beshalach, from its first phrase: when Pharaoh had let the people go. The short way, the verse says, was the way of the land of the Philistines, along the sea. It was near. And God led them another way, and the Torah gives the reason in God's own words: "Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt." Repent here means change their minds. People who had been slaves the day before weren't ready for a battle. One look at an army and Egypt would have seemed safe again. So God sends them the long way, through the wilderness, toward the sea, chosen for their sake, not for speed. The medieval philosopher Maimonides leaned on this verse. It shows, he said, how God works with human nature rather than against it. People can't leap from one way of life to its opposite overnight, so the Torah leads them gently, step by step, the way you'd lead someone who's frightened. He even used the verse to explain why the long years in the wilderness were needed: to raise a generation used to freedom. Notice what the long way isn't. It isn't avoidance. The sea is still coming, and so are hard days. It's a road sized to who you are right now, so you don't give up before you arrive.
screen: `BESHALACH: WHEN HE LET GO.` · `THE SHORT ROAD: PHILISTINE LAND.` · `LEST THEY SEE WAR AND TURN BACK.` · `MAIMONIDES: STEP BY STEP.` · then, large: `THE LONG WAY CAN BE KINDER.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're trying to change, a habit, a relationship, a part of yourself, and ask whether you've been taking the shortest road, all at once, and turning back every time it gets hard. Now picture a longer road instead: a smaller first step, a slower pace you could actually keep. Don't decide everything; just see the longer road, and notice whether it feels kinder.
Beshalach. When he let go. The portion of the sea, which opens with God choosing the long road so a frightened people won't turn back.
Your line: the long way can be kinder. Slow is not the same as stuck. See you tomorrow.

339.title: Beshalach: Joseph's bones (Exodus 13:19)
339.hook: while others gather silver, Moses carries Joseph's bones, keeping an old promise
339.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats keeping one's word as weighty, and promises to the dying especially so; Moses carrying Joseph's bones is often taught as the model of a promise kept across generations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long way round: God led a frightened people away from the short road. Your line was the long way can be kinder. Today, what Moses carries on that road.

Picture moving day after a hundred years in the same house. Everyone grabs what matters: the good dishes, the jewelry, the papers. And one person is up in the attic, looking for something nobody else remembers: a promise made long before any of them were born. The Israelites are leaving Egypt in a hurry, and the Torah stops, mid-march, for one short verse about what Moses chose to pack.
screen: `MOVING DAY, A HUNDRED YEARS ON.` → `EVERYONE GRABS WHAT MATTERS.` → `ONE PERSON IN THE ATTIC.`

segments.voice: "And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him." That's the verse. To hear why it matters, go back to the end of Genesis. Joseph, dying in Egypt, made his brothers swear: when God remembers you and brings you out, carry my bones up with you. Generations passed. Slavery came. Most people must have forgotten. Moses didn't. The Talmud sets a scene around the verse. On the night of leaving, the Israelites were busy with the silver and gold the Egyptians had given them; the Torah does say they asked for jewels of silver and gold, and received them. But Moses, the Talmud says, was busy with Joseph's bones, and it quotes a line from Proverbs about him: the wise in heart takes on commandments. Everyone else carried treasure. He carried a promise. The rabbis tell more: Joseph's coffin had been sunk in the Nile, and an old woman named Serach, Joseph's niece, remembered where. That part is midrash, a story the tradition tells, not the plain text. The plain text finishes the arc much later. In the book of Joshua, Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem, in the land. A promise made by brothers, kept by a descendant of one of them, finished by a generation not yet born. And the Hebrew word for bone, etzem, also means essence, the self. Moses carried Joseph's very self out of Egypt.
screen: `AND MOSES TOOK THE BONES.` · `JOSEPH'S OATH, END OF GENESIS.` · `SILVER FOR THEM, BONES FOR MOSES.` · `BURIED AT SHECHEM, AT LAST.` · then, large: `CARRY THE BONES.`

segments.voice: Let one old promise come up, even a small one: a call you meant to make, a recipe you meant to learn, the town your grandfather came from. Don't judge how long it has waited; Joseph's waited a long time too. Just hold it, and ask what one step would carry it a little further.
Beshalach. When he let go. Our portion, where Moses leaves Egypt carrying Joseph's bones, an old promise kept.
Your line: carry the bones. Some promises take generations to keep. Day three hundred thirty-nine, done.

340.title: Beshalach: stop praying, move (Exodus 14:15)
340.hook: at the sea, God asks Moses why he cries out, and tells the people to go forward
340.howItsDone: The crossing of the sea is read in synagogue twice a year: in the weekly portion Beshalach, and on the seventh day of Passover, which tradition dates to the night of the crossing. Nachshon is taught to children as the one who stepped in first.

segments.voice: Yesterday Moses carried Joseph's bones out of Egypt while others carried silver. Your line was carry the bones. Today, the sea in front of them, and an army behind.

An email drafted and never sent. A doctor's appointment someone keeps meaning to book. A thing gets worried about, maybe prayed about, until the thinking itself becomes a place to hide. Now the Israelites are trapped: the sea ahead, Pharaoh's chariots coming up behind. The people cry out in terror. Moses tells them to stand still and watch. And then God says something to Moses that sounds, at first, almost like a rebuke.
screen: `THE EMAIL YOU NEVER SEND.` → `SEA IN FRONT, CHARIOTS BEHIND.` → `GOD SPEAKS TO MOSES.`

segments.voice: God asks Moses why he is crying out. Then: "speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Here's the strange part. The Torah never shows Moses crying out. The people cried out, a few verses earlier, and Moses told them to be calm. So what is God answering? Rashi, the medieval commentator, says Moses was standing and praying silently, and God's reply means: this is not the time for long prayer; Israel is in danger. Move. Prayer isn't wrong. Moses prayed many times, and God listened. But prayer has a time, and so does walking. The rabbis also tell who took the first step. In the Talmud, Rabbi Judah says the tribes stood at the shore, each wanting someone else to go first. Then Nachshon, son of Amminadav, of the tribe of Judah, jumped into the water. In some tellings he waded in up to his neck, and only then did the sea split. That's midrash, a story the tradition tells about the gap between one verse and the next. The Torah itself simply says Moses lifted his rod, stretched his hand over the sea, and a strong east wind blew all night. The story keeps being told for the picture it leaves: the sea parting in front of someone already walking.
screen: `WHY DO YOU CRY OUT TO ME?` · `RASHI: NOT THE TIME FOR LONG PRAYER.` · `NACHSHON STEPS IN FIRST.` · `THE STRONG EAST WIND.` · then, large: `PRAY, THEN GO FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been circling. If you pray, pray about it now, briefly and honestly; if not, just name it clearly. Then picture only the first step, not the whole crossing: the first sentence of the email, the number dialed, the shoes put on, your foot touching the water.
Beshalach. When he let go. Our portion, where at the edge of the sea God tells Moses: speak to the people, and let them go forward.
Your line: pray, then go forward. Both have their time. That's day three hundred forty.

341.title: Beshalach: bitter water made sweet (Exodus 15:22–26)
341.hook: at Marah the water is bitter until a tree is thrown in
341.howItsDone: The Song at the Sea, sung just before the Marah story, is part of the daily morning service, and the words of Exodus 15:26 about the LORD who heals are echoed in Jewish prayers for healing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, still in Beshalach, God said go forward at the sea, and the rabbis told of Nachshon stepping in first. Your line was pray, then go forward. Today, three days past the sea, and thirsty.

Big wins have a strange aftertaste. The wedding ends and the thank-you notes begin. The new job starts and the commute is awful. The Israelites have just walked through the sea on dry land and sung a song that is still part of Jewish morning prayer. Three days later, in the wilderness of Shur, they still haven't found water. When they finally do, at a place called Marah, they lift it to their lips and spit it out.
screen: `THE WIN, THEN THE AFTERTASTE.` → `THREE DAYS, NO WATER.` → `MARAH: THEY SPIT IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Marah means bitter. The place is named for its water, and the people do what thirsty people do: they complain to Moses. What shall we drink? Moses cries out to God, and God shows him a tree, a piece of wood. Moses throws it in, and in the old Jewish translation, "the waters were made sweet." A few verses, that's all. The Torah doesn't say what kind of tree it was, and the rabbis couldn't resist asking. In the Mekhilta, an early commentary, several sages each name a different tree. One opinion says it was itself bitter: God can heal bitter with bitter. Another says the tree stands for the words of Torah, which the rabbis link to the tree of life in the book of Proverbs. Then the story ends with a line about God: "for I am the LORD that healeth thee." Notice what the story doesn't do. It doesn't scold them for being thirsty, or take them back to the sea. The bitterness is real; something is thrown into the middle of it, and it changes. Sometimes the change is a tree in the water: a meal someone brings, a joke at the right moment, an old song, a page of something wise. Small things, dropped into the bitter part.

segments.voice: Taste one bitter thing honestly, not the biggest, a smaller one: a tense email thread, a chore you hate, a sour mood between you and someone. Ask what small thing could be thrown into it, a kind word, a cup of tea, a walk, a song, and picture dropping it in. If you pray, you can hold the line from Marah: the LORD that healeth thee.

342.title: Beshalach: held-up hands (Exodus 17:8–13)
342.hook: when Moses' arms tire, Aaron and Hur hold them up until sunset
342.howItsDone: The Amalek story is read in synagogue on the morning of Purim, since Haman is traditionally linked to Amalek, and on the Shabbat before Purim the command to remember Amalek is read from Deuteronomy.

segments.voice: Yesterday at Marah, a tree thrown into bitter water made it sweet. Your line was a tree in the water. Today, the last day of Beshalach, and a battle.

Hold your arms straight out in front of you. Not for a few seconds; for a minute. Then imagine an afternoon. The shoulders burn first, then the forearms shake, and at some point the arms just drop, no matter how much you care. The Israelites are camped at a place called Rephidim when a people called Amalek attacks them. Joshua leads the fighters below. Moses climbs a hill with the staff of God in his hand. And the battle comes down to something as ordinary and human as tired arms.
screen: `ARMS OUT FOR A MINUTE.` → `THEN AN AFTERNOON.` → `AMALEK ATTACKS.`

segments.voice: When Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails. When he lets them down, Amalek prevails. And his hands get heavy. So two people step in: Aaron, his brother, and Hur, a man we barely meet anywhere else. They put a stone under Moses so he can sit, and they stand one on each side holding up his arms, "and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun." The word for steady, emunah, is the word usually translated faith. His hands were faithfulness, held up by friends. The Mishnah asks the obvious question: did Moses' hands win or lose a war? No, it says. When Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to their Father in heaven, they prevailed; when they didn't, they fell. The hands were a sign pointing up. The Talmud notices the stone. Why not a cushion? Because Moses wouldn't sit in comfort while his people were suffering in the fight. And Amalek becomes a name in Jewish memory. Deuteronomy says they struck at the weary and the stragglers at the rear, and in tradition Amalek comes to stand for cruelty that targets the weak. So Beshalach ends where it began, with a people learning to walk: the long way round, Joseph's bones, the sea, bitter water, and now Moses on a hill, held up by friends.

segments.voice: If you can, lift your arms a little and feel how soon they want to fall, then rest them. Think of someone holding something up all day, a parent caring for a child or an aging mother, a teacher, a nurse, a friend carrying a cause. Picture standing beside them like Aaron, or like Hur, and ask what holding up their arms would look like.
Amalek. The people who attacked Israel at Rephidim, striking at the weary, and the battle won while friends held up Moses' tired hands.
Your line: hold up the hands. Nobody is meant to hold them up alone. Until tomorrow.

343.title: Yitro: named for an outsider
343.hook: the portion with the Ten Words is named for Jethro, a Midianite priest
343.howItsDone: Yitro is read in synagogue in winter; when the Ten Commandments are chanted, people in some congregations stand. Jewish teachers point out that the portion is named for Jethro, a Midianite priest.

segments.voice: Yesterday Amalek attacked, and Aaron and Hur held up Moses' tired arms. Your line was hold up the hands. Today, a new portion, and a visitor.

A trivia question. Which portion of the Torah holds the Ten Commandments, the moment at Mount Sinai, thunder, smoke, the voice of God? And what's it called? Not Moses. Not Sinai. Not the Ten Words. It's named after Moses' father-in-law, a priest of Midian, who wasn't an Israelite at all. His name was Jethro; in Hebrew, Yitro. And before Sinai even comes into view, he walks into the camp and tells Moses he's doing his job wrong.
screen: `WHERE ARE THE TEN COMMANDMENTS?` → `NAMED FOR A PRIEST OF MIDIAN.` → `YITRO WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: Yitro has heard everything God did for Israel, and he comes to the wilderness bringing Moses' wife Zipporah and their two sons. Moses tells him the whole story, and Yitro rejoices, and blesses the God who rescued them. The next morning he watches Moses sit as judge for the people, from morning until evening, everyone lining up with their disputes. And he says, in the old Jewish translation: "The thing that thou doest is not good." You'll wear yourself out, and the people too. Then a plan. Find capable, honest, God-fearing people. Make them judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Let them handle the small cases and bring you the great ones. And Moses listens; he does what his father-in-law says. In the Torah's telling, Israel's courts are built on the advice of an outsider. Rashi, quoting the old midrash, says Yitro had seven names, and one of them, Yeter, means addition, because he added a section to the Torah. The rabbis even argued about the timing: did he come before Sinai, or after, with the Torah moving his story here? They didn't settle it. But there it sits, right before the Ten Words, and the portion carries his name. A tradition that names the portion of Sinai after a Midianite priest is saying something about where wisdom can come from.
screen: `YITRO REJOICES AND BLESSES.` · `THE THING THAT THOU DOEST IS NOT GOOD.` · `JUDGES OF THOUSANDS TO TENS.` · `MOSES LISTENS.` · then, large: `WISDOM FROM OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone outside your usual circle: a different generation, background, field or faith. Picture them watching you work from morning to evening, the way Yitro watched Moses, and ask what they might notice that you can't. Let the answer surprise you if it wants to.
Yitro. Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, priest of Midian, whose advice shaped Israel's courts and whose name is on the portion of the Ten Words.
Your line: wisdom from outside. A week of walking now: the sign on the hand, the long way, the bones, the sea, Marah, the held-up hands. That's day three hundred forty-three.
